collection.title: Noemorph philosophy, arguments, and historical traditions gap additions
collection.method: Exact-name and semantic gap audit against the 207-record base catalog, followed by source-level checking against primary works, primary-source translations, DOI records, and authoritative scholarly reference entries.
collection.source_policy: Each candidate retains at least two exact HTTPS locators. Summaries report source-attributable claims only; boundary notes identify common overextensions and translation risks.
collection.coverage_note: These are independent, provisional catalog candidates. The collection does not claim exhaustiveness and asserts no cross-record relationships, equivalences, or synthesis. Living and internally diverse traditions are represented through named texts and interpreters rather than as uniform civilizational views.

records.name: Knowledge argument (Mary thought experiment)
records.status_note: Jackson's 1982 formulation remains a central anti-physicalist argument, but ability, acquaintance, phenomenal-concept, and new-knowledge/old-fact replies dispute its conclusion; Jackson later rejected the argument's anti-physicalist use.
records.summary: Mary is stipulated to possess complete physical information about human color vision while lacking color experience. When she first sees color, she appears to learn what such experience is like; Jackson argued that this shows that not all information or facts are physical.
records.scope: Epistemic argument about whether complete physical knowledge exhausts phenomenal knowledge.
records.boundary_note: The thought experiment does not by itself identify a nonphysical substance or mechanism. A weaker conclusion about a new way of knowing may be accepted without accepting nonphysical facts.

claim_scope.applies_to: Claims that complete physical knowledge necessarily includes every fact or kind of knowledge about conscious experience.
claim_scope.does_not_establish: A specific ontology of qualia, substance dualism, or an empirical mechanism of consciousness.

evidence_profile.citation_mix: One original formulation and one peer-reviewed living reference entry.
evidence_profile.verification_summary: Primary DOI resolved; SEP locator and authorship checked.

open_questions: Does Mary acquire a new fact, a new concept, an ability, acquaintance, or only a new mode of presentation?
Can complete physical knowledge coherently be specified without already including phenomenal concepts?

citations.title: Qualia: The Knowledge Argument
citations.venue: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, substantive revision

records.name: Philosophical-zombie conceivability argument
records.status_note: Debate turns on ideal conceivability, the move from conceivability to metaphysical possibility, and whether a physical duplicate without experience is coherently specified.
records.summary: Chalmers argues that a molecule-for-molecule physical duplicate of a conscious person that lacks phenomenal experience is ideally conceivable; if such ideal conceivability entails metaphysical possibility, then physical truths do not metaphysically necessitate all phenomenal truths.
records.scope: Modal challenge to physicalist supervenience claims about phenomenal consciousness.
records.boundary_note: A philosophical zombie is a stipulated modal case, not an empirically detected organism. The argument depends on controversial bridge principles between conceivability and possibility.

claim_scope.applies_to: The claim that a complete physical duplicate must necessarily duplicate phenomenal consciousness.
claim_scope.does_not_establish: That zombies actually exist, that consciousness lacks physical correlates, or which nonphysical theory is correct.

evidence_profile.citation_mix: One author-maintained locator for the primary monograph and one SEP entry.
evidence_profile.verification_summary: Primary author page and SEP locator checked.

open_questions: What standard of ideal or positive conceivability is strong enough to support the modal inference?
Can phenomenal concepts explain the intuition of separability while preserving physical necessity?

citations.title: The Conscious Mind: In Search of a Fundamental Theory

records.name: Explanatory gap
records.status_note: Levine framed an explanatory or epistemic problem for materialist identities and did not treat the gap alone as a deductive refutation of materialism.
records.summary: Even if a pain state is identified with a neural or functional state, the physical description may appear not to explain why that state feels painful or why it has that qualitative character. Levine names this residual intelligibility problem the explanatory gap.
records.scope: Explanatory and epistemic adequacy of physical accounts of qualitative experience.
records.boundary_note: The explanatory gap is related to but not identical with Chalmers's later hard problem. It is a diagnosis of explanatory insufficiency and does not, without further premises, prove an ontological gap.

claim_scope.applies_to: Whether psychophysical identities make the qualitative character of experience intelligible.
claim_scope.does_not_establish: Property dualism, substance dualism, or the impossibility of future physical explanation.

evidence_profile.citation_mix: One original DOI-indexed article and one broad SEP orientation entry.
evidence_profile.verification_summary: Primary DOI resolved; SEP locator and authorship checked.

open_questions: Is the gap generated by phenomenal concepts, by limits of current science, or by a genuine ontological discontinuity?
What would count as closing rather than merely correlating across the gap?

citations.title: Materialism and Qualia: The Explanatory Gap

records.name: Chinese Room argument
records.tradition: Analytic philosophy of mind and artificial intelligence
records.status_note: Systems, robot, brain-simulator, other-minds, and virtual-mind replies dispute what follows from the room operator's lack of understanding.
records.summary: A person who understands no Chinese follows formal rules for transforming Chinese symbols and produces answers indistinguishable from those of a fluent speaker. Searle argues that successful symbol manipulation or program execution is not, by itself, sufficient for understanding or intentional content.
records.scope: Whether formal program execution is sufficient for linguistic understanding and intentional mentality.
records.boundary_note: Searle's target is the sufficiency claim associated with strong AI, not the proposition that no machine could think. The argument addresses understanding more directly than phenomenal consciousness.

claim_scope.applies_to: The claim that implementing the right formal program is sufficient for genuine understanding.
claim_scope.does_not_establish: That artificial systems cannot understand, that brains are noncomputational, or that phenomenal consciousness is nonphysical.

evidence_profile.citation_mix: One original article and one SEP entry surveying the argument and replies.
evidence_profile.verification_summary: Primary DOI resolved; SEP locator and authorship checked.

open_questions: Is understanding attributable to the whole system even if it is not attributable to the rule-following individual?
What role do embodiment, causal grounding, learning, and social use play in semantic understanding?

records.name: Thomistic intellective soul and reflexive self-knowledge
records.status: historically foundational · living Thomist reception · contested
records.status_note: The account remains active in Thomist philosophy but its metaphysics, interpretation of subsistence, and relation to contemporary mind science are disputed.
records.summary: Aquinas treats the human soul as the substantial form of a living human body while arguing that intellectual activity is not the act of a bodily organ. The intellect ordinarily knows itself through awareness of its own acts rather than through an immediate grasp of its essence.
records.scope: Aquinas's account of the human soul, immaterial intellectual operation, and intellectual self-knowledge.
records.boundary_note: This is a specifically Thomistic hylomorphic account, not generic Aristotelianism and not Cartesian substance dualism. Claims about postmortem subsistence belong to Aquinas's larger metaphysical and theological system.

claim_scope.applies_to: The unity of the living human being, the non-organic operation of intellect, and how intellect knows itself.
claim_scope.does_not_establish: A modern empirical theory of neural consciousness or a simple mind-body substance separation.

open_questions: How should Aquinas's claim that the soul is both form and subsistent be interpreted without importing Cartesian categories?
What is the exact phenomenological content, if any, of knowing one's act of understanding?

records.name: Averroes' unity of the material intellect
records.tradition: Andalusian Arabic Aristotelianism and Latin Averroist reception
records.status_note: The mature Long Commentary's unity thesis is clear enough to be a major interpretive locus, while Averroes' developmental views and the thesis's consequences for individual cognition remain debated.
records.summary: In the mature Long Commentary on Aristotle's De Anima, Averroes argues for a numerically single, separate material intellect and agent intellect shared by human thinkers. Individual acts of thinking nevertheless depend on bodily imaginative intentions supplied by particular people.
records.era: 12th century; Latin reception in the 13th–14th centuries
records.scope: The ontology and numerical unity of receptive intellect in Averroes' mature psychology.
records.boundary_note: The polemical label 'monopsychism' can mislead: the unity claim concerns intellect, not a claim that all people are one complete soul or person. Earlier and middle commentaries should not be collapsed into the mature position.

claim_scope.applies_to: The receptive and agent intellects and their relation to individualized imaginative cognition.
claim_scope.does_not_establish: A single shared phenomenal field, loss of bodily individuality, or a general doctrine that all souls are numerically one.

evidence_profile.citation_mix: Yale translation locator plus SEP historical orientation.
evidence_profile.verification_summary: Book DOI resolved; SEP locator and authorship checked.

open_questions: How do individual humans own or participate in thoughts if the receptive intellect is numerically one?
How sharply should the mature view be separated from Averroes' earlier commentaries?

records.name: Stoic corporeal psychology, impression and assent
records.status_note: The school developed across centuries and much early evidence survives through fragments and later reports; Chrysippus is especially important but should not stand for every Stoic phase.
records.summary: Stoics treat the soul as corporeal pneuma and locate the adult rational commanding faculty, the hegemonikon, within the embodied organism. Impressions present content; assent, withholding, impulse, and judgment are functions of the rational commanding faculty and are central to belief and action.
records.scope: Stoic accounts of the embodied soul, rational impressions, assent, impulse, and the commanding faculty.
records.boundary_note: Calling Stoicism 'materialist' must not import contemporary identity theory. Evidence is distributed across hostile and sympathetic reports, and later Stoic practical vocabularies do not always preserve early technical detail.

claim_scope.applies_to: Embodied psychic organization and the role of impression, assent, and impulse in rational agency.
claim_scope.does_not_establish: A single unchanged Stoic doctrine across all periods or a modern neuroscientific account of consciousness.

What evidential weight should be assigned to later doxographical reports about early Stoic localization of the hegemonikon?

records.name: Epicurean corporeal soul, sensation and mind
records.status_note: Epicurus' surviving letters and later Epicurean witnesses support the core corporeal account, while detailed reconstruction depends on fragmentary and transmitted texts.
records.summary: Epicurus describes the soul as a fine corporeal aggregate dispersed through the body and as a principal cause of sensation only while organized with the body. Later Epicurean exposition distinguishes rational mind from the soul distributed through the frame and treats both as mortal when their atoms disperse.
records.era: 4th century BCE–1st century BCE and later reception
records.scope: Epicurean atomist accounts of soul, mind, bodily organization, sensation, and death.
records.boundary_note: The record distinguishes Epicurus' surviving formulation from Lucretius' later exposition. Ancient atomism should not be redescribed as contemporary neural reductionism, and 'soul' here does not mean an incorporeal immortal substance.

claim_scope.applies_to: The material composition of soul, the body-soul conditions of sensation, and psychic mortality.
claim_scope.does_not_establish: Modern atomic neuroscience or that every later Epicurean retained an identical component model.

evidence_profile.citation_mix: University-hosted Letter to Herodotus excerpt plus specialist SEP entry.
evidence_profile.verification_summary: Columbia primary-text locator and SEP metadata checked.

open_questions: How should Epicurus' fine-particle account be separated from later Lucretian terminology for mind and soul?
What exactly individuates mental functions within the body-soul compound in the surviving evidence?

records.name: Mīmāṃsā rival accounts of self-awareness
aliases: Prābhākara tripuṭī-saṃvit and Kumārila's cognition theory
records.status_note: The entry deliberately preserves the opposition between Prābhākara and Bhāṭṭa Mīmāṃsā rather than inventing a single school view.
records.summary: Prābhākara theorists hold that a cognition manifests its object, the cognizing self, and itself together, often described as tripuṭī-saṃvit. Kumārila rejects direct self-cognition of cognition and instead explains awareness of cognition through its effects or the object's knownness, while defending an enduring subject.
records.scope: Competing Mīmāṃsā accounts of how cognition, object, and subject become known.
records.boundary_note: This is not one Mīmāṃsā theory. It should not be collapsed into Advaita's witness-consciousness vocabulary or Buddhist theories of reflexive awareness, despite partial overlap in translated terms.

claim_scope.applies_to: Whether and how cognition discloses itself, its object, and an enduring subject.
claim_scope.does_not_establish: A uniform Indian account of consciousness or identity between Mīmāṃsā and other South Asian self-awareness theories.

basis: two specialist authoritative scholarly reference entries
evidence_profile.citation_mix: SEP entries on Kumārila and personhood in classical Indian philosophy.
evidence_profile.verification_summary: Both SEP locators and authorship metadata checked.

open_questions: How should later Prābhākara and Bhāṭṭa refinements be split into separate versioned records?
Which Sanskrit technical terms should remain untranslated in UI labels to avoid false equivalence?

records.name: Nishida's pure experience and later self-awareness
records.tradition: Kyoto School and modern Japanese philosophy
records.status_note: Nishida's vocabulary and architecture changed substantially; the early pure-experience account and later work on self-awareness, place, and nothingness require phase-sensitive cataloging.
records.summary: In An Inquiry into the Good, Nishida presents pure experience as experience prior to the subject-object division, encompassing sensory and intellectual activity. His later philosophy reworks the problem through self-awareness (jikaku), place (basho), and the logic of nothingness rather than simply repeating the early formulation.
records.scope: Nishida's early account of pre-subject-object experience and its later philosophical transformations.
records.boundary_note: The record does not equate early pure experience with Nishida's entire mature system, reduce the philosophy to Zen doctrine, or identify Nishida's use of experience with William James's despite acknowledged influence.

claim_scope.applies_to: The emergence of subject-object differentiation and Nishida's changing accounts of self-awareness and place.
claim_scope.does_not_establish: A timeless Japanese theory of consciousness or a single doctrine unchanged across Nishida's career.

evidence_profile.citation_mix: Yale translation locator for the early work plus SEP developmental overview.
evidence_profile.verification_summary: Publisher metadata and SEP authorship checked.

open_questions: Which later texts should be registered separately for jikaku, basho, and absolute nothingness?
How should translations of keiken and jikaku preserve their distinct technical roles?

records.name: Xunzi's empty, unified and still heart-mind
records.status_note: The received Xunzi is composite and redactional questions remain; the account is best attributed to the text and its named authorial tradition with chapter-level precision.
records.summary: The Xunzi treats the heart-mind (xin) as the embodied center that knows, commands, desires, and judges. In 'Resolving Obsession,' apprehending the Way requires the heart-mind to be empty of fixed preoccupation, unified rather than divided, and still enough not to be disturbed by fantasy or distraction.
records.scope: The Xunzi's account of xin, cognitive distortion, attention, judgment, and disciplined knowing.
records.boundary_note: Xin should not be translated as a disembodied Cartesian mind. 'Empty' does not mean devoid of content; it describes freedom from prejudicial occupation while retaining prior knowledge.

claim_scope.applies_to: How fixation distorts judgment and how cultivated attention enables apprehension of the Way.
claim_scope.does_not_establish: A substance ontology of mind or a modern clinical theory of attention.

evidence_profile.citation_mix: Chinese Text Project primary chapter plus SEP scholarship.
evidence_profile.verification_summary: Exact chapter URL recorded; SEP metadata and authorship checked.

open_questions: Which psychological claims belong specifically to 'Resolving Obsession' rather than to the Xunzi corpus generally?
How should xin be displayed across translations without forcing a choice between 'heart' and 'mind'?

records.name: Tiantai contemplation of mind and three thousand realms in one thought
aliases: three thousand realms in a single thought-moment
records.tradition: Chinese Tiantai Buddhism and later Tiantai/Tendai traditions
records.status: historically foundational · living reception · interpretation contested
records.status_note: Doctrinal interpretation varies across Tiantai lineages and periods; the record concerns a named Zhiyi-centered framework rather than all Chinese Buddhist accounts of mind.
records.summary: Tiantai analysis associated with Zhiyi treats any moment of thought as involving the mutual inclusion of the three thousand dharmic realms and coordinates contemplation through the threefold truth of emptiness, provisional existence, and the middle. Mind is used as an accessible contemplative locus, not straightforwardly as a substance that manufactures an external world.
records.scope: Tiantai doctrines and practices concerning thought-moments, mutual inclusion, threefold truth, and contemplation of mind.
records.boundary_note: Do not flatten the doctrine into subjective idealism or the slogan 'mind creates matter.' Specialist scholarship emphasizes that mind has no unilateral ontological privilege over the dharmas it mutually includes.

claim_scope.applies_to: The structure and contemplation of experiential moments within Tiantai Buddhist soteriology.
claim_scope.does_not_establish: An empirical consciousness theory, a creator mind, or a doctrine shared by every East Asian Buddhist school.

evidence_profile.citation_mix: SEP tradition overview plus DOI-indexed analysis of mind and creation language.
evidence_profile.verification_summary: SEP locator checked; journal DOI resolved and retained.

open_questions: How should Zhiyi's own formulations be distinguished from later yinian sanqian systematization?
Which practice texts should be registered separately to keep doctrine, phenomenology, and ritual context distinct?

records.name: Al-Ghazālī's faculty psychology and heart-self vocabulary
aliases: Ghazalian psychology of qalb and nafs
records.tradition: Classical Islamic philosophy, theology and Sufism
records.status_note: Al-Ghazālī employs philosophical faculty theory alongside ethical, theological, and Sufi registers; the same term can function differently across works and passages.
records.summary: Al-Ghazālī describes sensory and internal faculties such as imagination, estimation, memory, and intellect while also using qalb, rūḥ, nafs, and ʿaql for bodily, psychic, ethical, and spiritual aspects of the person. In the Iḥyāʾ, the 'heart' can designate the bodily organ or the subtle knowing and morally responsible center, depending on context.
records.scope: Al-Ghazālī's internal-sense psychology and context-dependent vocabulary for the knowing, desiring, and morally cultivated self.
records.boundary_note: No single English word captures qalb, nafs, rūḥ, or ʿaql across contexts. The record is about al-Ghazālī, not an undifferentiated 'Islamic view,' and it keeps Avicennian philosophical analysis distinct from ethical-spiritual usage.

claim_scope.applies_to: Named faculties and the multiple registers in which al-Ghazālī analyzes cognition, desire, character, and inner knowledge.
claim_scope.does_not_establish: One stable component diagram for all of al-Ghazālī's works or a universal Muslim theory of consciousness.

evidence_profile.citation_mix: Publisher-verified Iḥyāʾ translation locator plus SEP historical analysis.
evidence_profile.verification_summary: Translation publication metadata and SEP authorship checked.

open_questions: How should differences among al-Ghazālī's philosophical, theological, and Iḥyāʾ vocabularies be versioned?
Which claims in later translations depend on choices among 'heart,' 'soul,' 'spirit,' 'self,' and 'intellect'?

records.name: Maimonidean unitary soul and intellectual perfection
records.tradition: Medieval Jewish Aristotelian philosophy in Arabic intellectual context
records.status_note: The unity of the soul and its faculties is textually explicit, while the precise account of active intellect, prophecy, conjunction, and individual immortality remains interpretively disputed.
records.summary: Maimonides presents the human soul as one soul with nutritive, sensory, imaginative, appetitive, and rational faculties rather than as several souls. Intellectual perfection is central to human fulfillment, and the active intellect figures in his accounts of perfected knowledge and prophecy.
records.scope: Maimonides' unitary faculty psychology and the role of intellect in human perfection and prophecy.
records.boundary_note: This is a Maimonidean Jewish-Aristotelian account shaped by Arabic philosophy, not a single Jewish doctrine. Strong claims about personal immortality or conjunction with the active intellect require separate textual adjudication.

claim_scope.applies_to: The unity and faculties of the human soul and their role in intellectual and prophetic perfection.
claim_scope.does_not_establish: A consensus Jewish account of mind or an uncontested theory of individual postmortem survival.

records.name: Yorùbá conceptions of person: ara, ẹ̀mí, orí and ọkàn
records.status: living tradition · active scholarship · internally contested
records.status_note: Named Yorùbá scholars offer overlapping but nonidentical analyses; component counts, translations, and the roles assigned to orí, ẹ̀mí, ọkàn, ara, and ìwà vary by source and context.
records.summary: Scholarly articulations of Yorùbá personhood analyze ènìyàn through terms including ara (body), ẹ̀mí (life-breath or life principle), orí or orí-inú (inner head, personal orientation, or destiny), ọkàn (with cognitive and affective uses), and ìwà (character or mode of being). Their boundaries and relations are disputed rather than fixed in a single canonical component chart.
records.scope: Named scholarly analyses of Yorùbá concepts used to describe embodied personhood, life, thought and feeling, destiny, agency, and character.
records.boundary_note: There is no warrant for presenting one frozen component list as 'the African mind.' English glosses such as soul, mind, spirit, personality, and destiny are interpretive and should remain linked to the author and linguistic context that uses them.

claim_scope.type: situated comparative-philosophical scholarship on a living tradition
claim_scope.applies_to: Named Yorùbá concepts of personhood as analyzed by specified scholars and sources.
claim_scope.does_not_establish: A uniform view held by every Yorùbá person, a pan-African ontology, or exact equivalence with Western mind-body categories.

evidence_profile.citation_mix: A Yorùbá philosopher's monograph and a DOI-indexed Yorùbá-perspective article.
evidence_profile.verification_summary: Book identity and table-of-contents scope checked; journal DOI resolved.

open_questions: How do regional, religious, gendered, and diasporic contexts alter the use of these person terms?
Which interpretations are linguistic descriptions, philosophical reconstructions, or claims grounded in ritual and oral knowledge?

records.name: Anishinaabe Place-Thought and human/nonhuman agency in Vanessa Watts
records.tradition: Anishinaabe and Haudenosaunee scholarship; related Neshnabék articulation
records.status: living situated articulation · anti-universalizing boundary required
records.status_note: The record is anchored to Vanessa Watts's named argument and uses Kimmerer only as a related Neshnabék articulation, not as interchangeable evidence for every Anishinaabe or Indigenous nation.
records.summary: Watts articulates Place-Thought as an Indigenous account in which land is alive and thinking and agency circulates through human and nonhuman worlds rather than belonging exclusively to humans. Kimmerer's related discussion of the grammar of animacy shows how language can sustain recognition of plants and other beings as active relations rather than inert objects.
proponents: Robin Wall Kimmerer as a related Neshnabék articulator
records.scope: Named, place-specific Indigenous scholarly articulations of land, thought, language, and human/nonhuman agency.
records.boundary_note: This is not a universal 'Indigenous ontology,' a generic animism category, or a claim that publication exhausts community knowledge. Nation, author, story, language, land, governance, and colonial context must remain attached to each claim.

claim_scope.applies_to: Watts's account of Place-Thought and a clearly marked related discussion of grammatical animacy by Kimmerer.
claim_scope.does_not_establish: Uniform belief across Indigenous peoples, scientific evidence that all matter is conscious, or equivalence among distinct nations' knowledge systems.

evidence_profile.citation_mix: University-repository copy of Watts's article plus Kimmerer's DOI-indexed article.
evidence_profile.verification_summary: Repository metadata and article abstract checked; Kimmerer DOI resolved.

open_questions: What permissions and community review are appropriate before adding oral, ceremonial, legal, or land-specific knowledge beyond published scholarship?
How should the catalog represent related but nonidentical Anishinaabe, Haudenosaunee, Potawatomi, and broader Neshnabék contexts without collapsing them?
